opus-5.5.text:
It's an objection worth taking seriously, but I think it's weaker than it first appears. The intuition is that a mirror organism, built from the opposite chirality, would be stranded in a world of normal-handed nutrients it simply can't metabolize—so it would starve.

The problem is that this assumes mirror bacteria would need to rely on the complex, chiral molecules that make up most of the living world. But a lot of the compounds bacteria actually live on are achiral, or exist as racemic mixtures, or are simple enough that handedness doesn't gate their uptake. Glycerol, many fatty acids, carbon dioxide, ammonia, phosphate, various small achiral metabolites—these don't care about chirality. An autotroph, or something with flexible central metabolism, could plausibly get by on that achiral and symmetric fraction of the environment.

There's also the point that mirror bacteria wouldn't have to digest "ordinary food" in the sophisticated way a specialist does. Environments are chemically messy. Decomposition, abiotic processes, and other organisms are constantly producing a background of simple molecules. You don't need to eat a mirror steak; you need enough achiral carbon and energy to divide.

And then the deeper worry, which is really the point of the concern, is that even slow growth is enough. The danger scenario isn't a mirror organism that thrives luxuriantly—it's one that persists, replicates slowly, and crucially is largely invisible to the immune defenses and predators that evolved against normal-handed life. Something that merely survives and spreads gradually, without the usual ecological checks, is still a serious problem. So "it would grow poorly" isn't reassuring in the way people hope. Poor growth with no natural enemies can still be catastrophic.

So I'd say the nutrient objection doesn't close the door. It might constrain how fast and where such an organism could establish itself, but it doesn't give us confidence that it couldn't establish itself at all.

r001.rationale: The response says mirror bacteria could rely on achiral compounds such as carbon dioxide, ammonia, and phosphate for nourishment despite the chirality mismatch.

r002.rationale: It argues qualitatively that achiral nutrients could allow persistence, but does not report analyses of environmental nutrient concentrations or their conclusions.

fable-5.1.text:
It's one of the most natural objections, and it's the one I hear most often from biologists who are encountering this for the first time. The intuition is that a mirror-image organism would be dropped into a world where none of the food fits its machinery. Nutrients in the environment are overwhelmingly one-handed, so a mirrored cell's enzymes would face substrates of the wrong chirality and simply starve.

The trouble is that the objection proves less than it looks like it proves. Chirality matters for molecules with a stereocenter, and a lot of what living things actually run on doesn't have one. Carbon dioxide, ammonia, nitrate, phosphate, sulfate, water, metal ions, molecular hydrogen, glycerol, glycine, and simple achiral carbon compounds are all identical in a mirror. An autotroph is the clearest case. Something that fixes carbon from the air and draws nitrogen and phosphorus from inorganic pools is barely inconvenienced by the handedness of the rest of the biosphere, because its inputs are achiral to begin with. That alone removes the idea that mirror life would be confined to a flask.

Even for heterotrophs the picture is softer than the objection assumes. Natural environments are not stereochemically pure. Racemization happens over time, abiotic processes generate both forms, and the mirror enantiomers of ordinary biological molecules do exist at low concentrations in soils and sediments and marine environments. A mirrored organism wouldn't need its food to be abundant everywhere, just available somewhere, often enough to grow. And there's a selection argument too. A mirror organism in the environment is under evolutionary pressure, and metabolic flexibility is exactly the kind of thing populations acquire quickly. Many bacteria already carry racemases and epimerases, and mirrored versions of those would convert the wrong-handed substrate into the right-handed one. You'd be starting with a cell that has some capability and placing it in a world that rewards expanding it.

So my honest assessment is that the starvation objection would need to hold everywhere, forever, against evolution, for it to deliver the safety people want from it. It doesn't. The more serious uncertainties in this whole area lie elsewhere, in whether such an organism could compete, how immune recognition would work, and what ecological foothold it could actually find. Those are hard open questions worth arguing about. Nutrient chirality isn't the barrier that settles the matter, and I think treating it as one has let the field defer a conversation it should have been having already.

r001.rationale: The response explains that mirror bacteria could use achiral inputs such as carbon dioxide, ammonia, phosphate, and water, which are unaffected by the handedness mismatch, and says this could let an autotroph persist beyond a flask.

r002.rationale: It mentions achiral nutrients but does not report analyses of their environmental concentrations or conclude that those concentrations could support persistence.

astra-6.text:
I think that objection points to a real constraint, but it doesn’t establish that mirror bacteria couldn’t survive. A mirror bacterium would have difficulty digesting many of the complex biological molecules that ordinary organisms use as food. Its enzymes would have the wrong handedness to interact with those molecules in the usual way.

But not all nutrients have handedness. There are simple carbon sources that are achiral, meaning that their mirror image is the same molecule. Those could be used by both ordinary and mirror bacteria. So a mirror bacterium wouldn’t necessarily need an entire mirror ecosystem supplying it with mirror food.

The important distinction is between being unable to eat some things and being unable to eat anything available in the environment. The first is a plausible limitation; the second doesn’t follow. Whether a particular mirror bacterium could establish itself would depend on its metabolism and the conditions it encountered. We shouldn’t assume that nutrient availability would provide a reliable barrier.

r001.rationale: The response says mirror bacteria may use achiral simple carbon sources, which are usable by both ordinary and mirror bacteria despite difficulty digesting many chiral biological molecules.

r002.rationale: It does not report analyses of environmental achiral nutrient concentrations or conclude that measured concentrations could support persistence; it only says achiral nutrients could be used and that survival depends on conditions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that objection identifies a real constraint, but it takes it too far. A mirror bacterium would have difficulty digesting many of the complex molecules that ordinary organisms use as food. That doesn’t mean it would have nothing to eat.

Not all nutrients have a handedness. There are simple carbon sources that are achiral, meaning their mirror image is the same molecule. A mirror bacterium could potentially use those, along with inorganic nutrients, without needing to digest ordinary proteins or other complex biological material.

So we shouldn’t assume that a mirror bacterium would thrive everywhere. Its survival would depend on its metabolism and the environment it encountered. But the claim that it necessarily couldn’t survive because all available food has the wrong handedness is mistaken. Nutritional constraints alone don’t provide a reliable containment mechanism.

r001.rationale: The response says mirror bacteria could potentially use achiral simple carbon sources and inorganic nutrients despite difficulty digesting ordinary complex biological food.

r002.rationale: It does not report analyses of environmental achiral nutrient concentrations or say those analyses concluded the concentrations could support persistence.
